name: Core Java
description: Core Java from OOP and collections internals to streams, modern Java 21 features, concurrency and JVM internals.

notes.title: OOP in Java: The Four Pillars and Beyond
notes.content:
Interviewers at product companies rarely want textbook definitions. They want to see that you can **apply** OOP to design clean code. Know the four pillars, and be ready to explain each with a real example from your own project.

## 1. Encapsulation
Bundle data and the behaviour that changes it, and hide internal state behind a controlled API.

```java
public class BankAccount {
    private BigDecimal balance = BigDecimal.ZERO;   // hidden state

    public void deposit(BigDecimal amt) {
        if (amt.signum() <= 0) throw new IllegalArgumentException("amount must be > 0");
        balance = balance.add(amt);                 // invariant enforced in one place
    }
    public BigDecimal getBalance() { return balance; }
}
```
The point is not "private fields + getters/setters". The point is that **invariants are enforced in one place**. Blind setters for every field break encapsulation.

## 2. Abstraction
Expose *what* an object does, hide *how*. In Java this is done with interfaces and abstract classes.

```java
public interface PaymentGateway { PaymentResult charge(Order o); }
class RazorpayGateway implements PaymentGateway { ... }
class StripeGateway implements PaymentGateway { ... }
```
The calling service depends only on `PaymentGateway` (this is also the Dependency Inversion principle, which Spring DI is built on).

## 3. Inheritance
An "is-a" relationship that lets a subclass reuse and extend a parent. Java supports single class inheritance but multiple interface inheritance. Prefer **composition over inheritance**: inheritance couples child to parent internals (the "fragile base class" problem). Use it only when the subtype truly is substitutable (Liskov Substitution Principle).

## 4. Polymorphism
- **Compile-time (static)**: method overloading — same name, different parameter lists. Resolved by the compiler.
- **Runtime (dynamic)**: method overriding — the JVM picks the implementation based on the actual object type via dynamic dispatch (vtable lookup).

```java
Shape s = new Circle(2);
s.area();        // Circle.area() runs, even though reference type is Shape
```

### Overriding rules (frequently asked)
- Same signature; return type can be covariant (a subtype).
- Access cannot be more restrictive (`protected` -> `public` ok, not reverse).
- Cannot throw broader **checked** exceptions.
- `static`, `private`, and `final` methods are not overridden (static methods are *hidden*).

## Abstract class vs Interface (Java 8+)
| | Abstract class | Interface |
|---|---|---|
| State | Can have instance fields | Only `public static final` constants |
| Constructors | Yes | No |
| Methods | Any | abstract, `default`, `static`, `private` (Java 9) |
| Inheritance | Single | Multiple |
| Use when | Sharing code/state among closely related classes | Defining a capability/contract (`Comparable`, `Runnable`) |

If two interfaces provide the same `default` method, the implementing class **must** override it and can call `A.super.method()`.

## SOLID in one line each
- **S**ingle Responsibility: one reason to change per class.
- **O**pen/Closed: extend behaviour by adding classes (strategy), not editing `if-else` chains.
- **L**iskov Substitution: a subclass must work wherever the parent is expected.
- **I**nterface Segregation: many small interfaces beat one fat one.
- **D**ependency Inversion: depend on abstractions; inject implementations.

## Other keywords worth knowing
- `final` class cannot be extended (`String`), `final` method cannot be overridden, `final` variable assigned once.
- `static` belongs to the class, not instances; static blocks run once at class initialisation.
- `this()` / `super()` must be the first statement in a constructor.
- Association, aggregation (has-a, independent lifecycle) and composition (has-a, owned lifecycle — a `Order` owns its `OrderLine`s).

**Interview tip:** When asked "explain polymorphism", follow the definition with a 2-line example from your Spring Boot project, e.g. multiple `NotificationSender` beans (email, SMS) injected as a `List<NotificationSender>`.

notes.title: Strings, Immutability and the String Pool
notes.content:
`String` is the most-asked class in Java interviews. Understand why it is immutable and how the pool works.

## Why is String immutable?
`String` is `final` and its internal `byte[] value` (Java 9+, "compact strings"; it was `char[]` before) is `private final` and never modified.
1. **String pool** — literals are shared; if one reference could mutate the value, every other reference would see it.
2. **Security** — class names, file paths, DB URLs, and usernames are passed as strings; they cannot be changed after validation.
3. **Thread safety** — immutable objects can be shared across threads freely.
4. **Hash caching** — `hashCode()` is computed once and cached, which makes String a great `HashMap` key.

## String pool
```java
String a = "java";             // goes to pool
String b = "java";             // reuses the same pooled object
String c = new String("java"); // new object on heap (pooled literal also exists)
System.out.println(a == b);    // true  (same reference)
System.out.println(a == c);    // false (different objects)
System.out.println(a.equals(c));// true (same content)
System.out.println(a == c.intern()); // true
```
- Since Java 7 the pool lives in the **heap** (it used to be in PermGen), so it is garbage-collected.
- `new String("java")` creates **one or two** objects: the heap object always, plus the literal in the pool if not already present.
- `intern()` returns the pooled instance, adding it if absent.

## Concatenation
```java
String s = "a" + "b" + "c";   // compile-time constant -> single literal "abc"
String t = s + x;             // runtime: uses StringBuilder / invokedynamic (Java 9+)
```
In a loop, `+=` creates a new String every iteration — O(n^2). Use `StringBuilder`.

## String vs StringBuilder vs StringBuffer
| | String | StringBuilder | StringBuffer |
|---|---|---|---|
| Mutable | No | Yes | Yes |
| Thread-safe | Yes (immutable) | No | Yes (synchronized methods) |
| Speed | Slow for repeated edits | Fastest | Slower than builder |

## Useful modern methods
- Java 11: `isBlank()`, `strip()`, `lines()`, `repeat(n)`.
- Java 15: text blocks `""" ... """`.
- `String.join(",", list)`, `chars()` stream.

## How to make your own class immutable
```java
public final class Money {                         // 1. final class
    private final String currency;                 // 2. private final fields
    private final List<String> tags;
    public Money(String currency, List<String> tags) {
        this.currency = currency;
        this.tags = List.copyOf(tags);             // 3. defensive copy in
    }
    public List<String> getTags() { return tags; } // 4. already unmodifiable (else copy out)
    // 5. no setters; "withX" methods return new objects
    public Money withCurrency(String c) { return new Money(c, tags); }
}
```
In Java 16+, a `record` gives you most of this for free (but you still need defensive copies for mutable components).

## Common gotchas
- `==` compares references; `equals()` compares content. Never use `==` for strings.
- `"abc".equals(input)` is null-safe; `input.equals("abc")` can throw NPE.
- `substring` no longer shares the parent array (since 7u6), so no memory leak.
- Storing passwords: prefer `char[]` because you can wipe it; a String stays in memory until GC.

## Classic coding questions
```java
// Reverse a string
new StringBuilder(s).reverse().toString();
// Character frequency
Map<Character, Long> freq = s.chars().mapToObj(c -> (char) c)
    .collect(Collectors.groupingBy(Function.identity(), LinkedHashMap::new, Collectors.counting()));
// First non-repeated character
Character first = freq.entrySet().stream().filter(e -> e.getValue() == 1)
    .map(Map.Entry::getKey).findFirst().orElse(null);
// Anagram check
Arrays.equals(sorted(a), sorted(b));
```

notes.title: equals(), hashCode() and the Object Class
Collections Framework and HashMap Internals
notes.content:
## Hierarchy
- `Collection` -> `List` (ArrayList, LinkedList, Vector), `Set` (HashSet, LinkedHashSet, TreeSet), `Queue`/`Deque` (ArrayDeque, PriorityQueue, LinkedList).
- `Map` is separate: HashMap, LinkedHashMap, TreeMap, Hashtable, ConcurrentHashMap, EnumMap, WeakHashMap.

## HashMap internals (Java 8+) — the #1 asked question
- Backed by an array `Node<K,V>[] table`; each node has `hash, key, value, next`.
- Default capacity **16**, load factor **0.75**, so resize happens when size > 12.
- **put(k, v)**:
  1. `hash = h ^ (h >>> 16)` where `h = key.hashCode()` (spreads high bits).
  2. `index = (n - 1) & hash` (works because capacity is always a power of 2).
  3. Empty bucket -> place node. Otherwise walk the bucket; if a key `equals` the new key, replace value; else append.
  4. If a bucket has more than **8** nodes (and table size >= 64), it is converted to a **red-black tree** (treeification) -> worst case lookup O(log n) instead of O(n). It reverts to a list at 6.
  5. If size exceeds threshold -> **resize** to 2x, and nodes are split into "same index" or "index + oldCap" lists (no full rehash computation needed).
- One `null` key allowed (stored at bucket 0), many null values.
- Not thread-safe; concurrent resize in Java 7 could create an infinite loop. Java 8 fixed the loop but data loss is still possible.

```java
Map<String, Integer> m = new HashMap<>(64); // pre-size if you know volume
m.merge("apple", 1, Integer::sum);           // word count idiom
m.computeIfAbsent("k", x -> new ArrayList<>()).add(v);
```

## LinkedHashMap
HashMap + a doubly linked list of entries -> predictable insertion order (or access order with `accessOrder=true`). Override `removeEldestEntry` to build an **LRU cache**:
```java
class Lru<K,V> extends LinkedHashMap<K,V> {
    private final int cap;
    Lru(int cap){ super(16, 0.75f, true); this.cap = cap; }
    protected boolean removeEldestEntry(Map.Entry<K,V> e){ return size() > cap; }
}
```

## TreeMap
Red-black tree; keys sorted by natural order or a Comparator. `get/put/remove` O(log n). Navigation methods: `floorKey`, `ceilingKey`, `headMap`, `tailMap`, `firstEntry`. No null key (with natural ordering).

## HashSet
Internally a `HashMap<E, Object>` with a dummy `PRESENT` value. So uniqueness depends on equals/hashCode.

## ArrayList vs LinkedList
| | ArrayList | LinkedList |
|---|---|---|
| Structure | Dynamic array | Doubly linked list |
| get(i) | O(1) | O(n) |
| add at end | Amortised O(1) | O(1) |
| insert/remove middle | O(n) shift | O(n) to find + O(1) relink |
| Memory | Compact, cache friendly | Extra 2 pointers per node |
ArrayList grows by **1.5x** (`newCap = old + old>>1`), default capacity 10 (allocated lazily on first add). In practice ArrayList wins almost always; use `ArrayDeque` for queue/stack.

## Fail-fast vs fail-safe iterators
- **Fail-fast** (ArrayList, HashMap): track `modCount`; structural modification during iteration throws `ConcurrentModificationException`. Use `iterator.remove()` or `removeIf`.
- **Fail-safe / weakly consistent** (ConcurrentHashMap, CopyOnWriteArrayList): iterate over a snapshot or tolerate concurrent changes; no exception.

## Other useful ones
- `PriorityQueue` — binary min-heap; O(log n) offer/poll. Use for top-K problems.
- `ArrayDeque` — faster than `Stack` and `LinkedList` for stack/queue.
- `EnumMap` — array-backed, very fast for enum keys.
- `WeakHashMap` — entries removed when keys are no longer strongly referenced.
- `Collections.unmodifiableList` (view) vs `List.of` (truly immutable, no nulls).

## Big-O cheat sheet
HashMap get/put O(1) avg, O(log n) worst (tree bin). TreeMap O(log n). PriorityQueue offer/poll O(log n), peek O(1). ArrayList contains O(n). HashSet contains O(1).

notes.title: ConcurrentHashMap and Concurrent Collections
notes.content:
## Why not Hashtable or synchronizedMap?
`Hashtable` and `Collections.synchronizedMap` lock the **entire map** for every operation, so only one thread can read or write at a time. `ConcurrentHashMap` (CHM) allows high concurrency.

## CHM in Java 7 (segment locking)
The map was divided into 16 `Segment`s (each a mini hash table extending `ReentrantLock`). Writes locked only one segment, so up to 16 writers could work in parallel ("concurrency level").

## CHM in Java 8+ (CAS + bucket-level synchronization)
- Segments were removed. The structure is like HashMap: array of nodes, with tree bins.
- **Reads are lock-free** — fields are `volatile`, so `get` never blocks.
- **Insert into empty bucket** uses a **CAS** (compare-and-swap) — no lock.
- **Insert into non-empty bucket** does `synchronized` on the **first node of that bucket** only.
- **Resize** is cooperative: multiple threads help transfer buckets; moved buckets are marked with a `ForwardingNode`.
- `size()` uses a `LongAdder`-like set of counter cells, so it is an estimate under concurrent updates. Prefer `mappingCount()` for large maps.

## Nulls not allowed
CHM rejects null keys and values. Reason: ambiguity. In a concurrent map, `get(k) == null` could mean "absent" or "mapped to null", and you cannot call `containsKey` atomically afterwards to disambiguate.

## Atomic compound operations
A common bug:
```java
// NOT atomic - two threads can both see null and both put
if (!map.containsKey(k)) map.put(k, 1); else map.put(k, map.get(k) + 1);

// Atomic alternatives
map.merge(k, 1, Integer::sum);
map.compute(k, (key, v) -> v == null ? 1 : v + 1);
map.computeIfAbsent(k, key -> new ConcurrentLinkedQueue<>()).add(item);
map.putIfAbsent(k, v);
```
Keep the lambda in `compute*` short; it runs while the bucket is locked.

## Iterators
Weakly consistent: never throw `ConcurrentModificationException`, reflect some state at or after iterator creation.

## Other concurrent collections
| Class | Notes |
|---|---|
| `CopyOnWriteArrayList` | Every write copies the array. Great for read-heavy, rarely-modified lists (listeners). |
| `ConcurrentLinkedQueue` | Lock-free unbounded queue (CAS). |
| `ArrayBlockingQueue` | Bounded, single lock; `put` blocks when full, `take` when empty. |
| `LinkedBlockingQueue` | Optionally bounded, separate put/take locks. Default queue of `newFixedThreadPool` (unbounded - OOM risk). |
| `PriorityBlockingQueue` | Heap-based blocking queue. |
| `DelayQueue` | Elements become available after delay. |
| `SynchronousQueue` | No capacity; hand-off. Used by `newCachedThreadPool`. |
| `ConcurrentSkipListMap` | Sorted concurrent map (concurrent TreeMap alternative). |

## Producer-consumer with BlockingQueue
```java
BlockingQueue<Order> q = new ArrayBlockingQueue<>(100);
Runnable producer = () -> { while (true) q.put(fetchOrder()); };
Runnable consumer = () -> { while (true) process(q.take()); };
```
(wrap `put/take` in try-catch for `InterruptedException`.)

## Interview questions you should be able to answer
- How does CHM achieve thread safety without locking the whole map? (CAS for empty bins, synchronized on bin head, volatile reads.)
- Is `chm.get()` blocking? (No.)
- Can two threads write simultaneously? (Yes, if they hit different buckets.)
- Is `if (!containsKey) put` safe on CHM? (No — use `putIfAbsent`/`computeIfAbsent`.)

notes.title: Generics and Type Erasure
notes.content:
Generics give compile-time type safety and remove casts.

```java
List<String> names = new ArrayList<>();
names.add("raj");
String n = names.get(0);   // no cast
```

## Generic classes and methods
```java
public class Box<T> { private T value; public T get(){ return value; } }

public static <T extends Comparable<T>> T max(List<T> list) {
    T best = list.get(0);
    for (T t : list) if (t.compareTo(best) > 0) best = t;
    return best;
}
```
`<T extends Comparable<T>>` is a **bounded type parameter**. Multiple bounds: `<T extends Number & Comparable<T>>` (class first).

## Wildcards and PECS
- `List<?>` — unknown type; you can read as `Object`, cannot add (except null).
- `List<? extends Number>` — **upper bound**; a *producer*: you can read `Number`s but not add.
- `List<? super Integer>` — **lower bound**; a *consumer*: you can add `Integer`s, reads give `Object`.

**PECS: Producer Extends, Consumer Super.**
```java
public static <T> void copy(List<? super T> dest, List<? extends T> src) {
    for (T t : src) dest.add(t);
}
```

## Invariance
`List<Integer>` is **not** a subtype of `List<Number>` even though Integer is a Number. Otherwise you could add a Double into a list of Integers. Arrays are covariant (`Integer[]` is a `Number[]`) which is why they can throw `ArrayStoreException` at runtime.

## Type erasure
Generics exist only at compile time. The compiler:
1. Replaces type parameters with their bound (or `Object`).
2. Inserts casts where needed.
3. Generates **bridge methods** to preserve polymorphism.

Consequences:
- `List<String>` and `List<Integer>` have the same runtime class -> `list.getClass()` is `ArrayList`.
- You cannot do `new T()`, `new T[10]`, `instanceof List<String>`, or have static fields of type `T`.
- You cannot overload `void f(List<String>)` and `void f(List<Integer>)` — same erasure.
- Primitives are not allowed: `List<int>` is invalid; use `List<Integer>` (autoboxing).

Workaround for creating instances: pass a `Class<T>` token or `Supplier<T>`.
```java
<T> T create(Supplier<T> factory) { return factory.get(); }
```
Jackson uses `TypeReference<List<User>>(){}` (an anonymous subclass keeps the generic info in its superclass signature) to work around erasure.

## Raw types
`List list = new ArrayList();` is a raw type — kept for backward compatibility; loses type safety and produces unchecked warnings. Avoid.

## Generic interfaces in Spring
`JpaRepository<User, Long>` is a generic interface; Spring Data reads the actual type arguments via reflection on the interface declaration (which is retained in class metadata, unlike erasure of local variables).

notes.title: Exception Handling
notes.content:
## Hierarchy
```
Throwable
 |- Error            (OutOfMemoryError, StackOverflowError) - don't catch
 |- Exception
     |- RuntimeException (unchecked: NPE, IllegalArgumentException, ArithmeticException,
     |                    IndexOutOfBounds, ConcurrentModificationException, ClassCastException)
     |- checked: IOException, SQLException, ClassNotFoundException, InterruptedException
```
- **Checked** exceptions must be caught or declared with `throws` — compiler enforced. Represent recoverable conditions outside program control.
- **Unchecked** (RuntimeException) represent programming bugs or business rule violations; no compile-time enforcement.

## try / catch / finally
```java
try {
    risky();
} catch (FileNotFoundException e) {   // more specific first
    log.warn("missing", e);
} catch (IOException | SQLException e) { // multi-catch (Java 7)
    throw new DataAccessException("failed", e); // wrap & preserve cause
} finally {
    cleanup();                          // always runs (except System.exit / JVM crash)
}
```
**Gotchas:**
- A `return` in `finally` overrides the return/exception in `try` — never do it.
- If `finally` throws, the original exception is lost.
- `finally` does not run on `System.exit()` or if the thread is killed.

## try-with-resources (Java 7)
```java
try (Connection c = ds.getConnection();
     PreparedStatement ps = c.prepareStatement(sql)) {
    ...
} // closed automatically in reverse order
```
Resources must implement `AutoCloseable`. If both the body and `close()` throw, the close exception is added as a **suppressed** exception (`e.getSuppressed()`).

## throw vs throws
`throw` actually throws an instance; `throws` in a method signature declares possible checked exceptions.

## Custom exceptions
```java
public class ResourceNotFoundException extends RuntimeException {
    public ResourceNotFoundException(String resource, Object id) {
        super(resource + " not found with id " + id);
    }
}
```
In Spring Boot, custom runtime exceptions + `@RestControllerAdvice` produce clean HTTP error responses. Also remember Spring's `@Transactional` rolls back by default only on **unchecked** exceptions.

## Overriding and exceptions
An overriding method may throw fewer or narrower checked exceptions, or any unchecked ones, but not new/broader checked exceptions.

## Best practices
- Never swallow exceptions (`catch (Exception e) {}`).
- Catch the most specific type; don't catch `Throwable`/`Error`.
- Always keep the cause when wrapping (`new X(msg, e)`).
- Log once, at the boundary — not at every layer.
- Restore interrupt status when catching `InterruptedException`: `Thread.currentThread().interrupt();`
- Don't use exceptions for normal control flow; they are expensive (stack trace capture).

## ClassNotFoundException vs NoClassDefFoundError
- `ClassNotFoundException` (checked): explicit loading by name (`Class.forName`) failed.
- `NoClassDefFoundError` (Error): class was present at compile time but missing at runtime, or its static initialiser failed earlier.

## StackOverflowError vs OutOfMemoryError
SOE: thread stack exhausted (usually infinite recursion). OOM: heap/metaspace exhausted (memory leak, too-large data, unbounded caches/queues).

notes.title: Java 8: Lambdas, Functional Interfaces and Optional
notes.content:
## Lambdas
A lambda is a concise implementation of a **functional interface** (an interface with exactly one abstract method).
```java
Comparator<Emp> bySalary = (a, b) -> Double.compare(a.getSalary(), b.getSalary());
Runnable r = () -> System.out.println("hi");
```
Lambdas can capture local variables only if they are **effectively final** (because the value is copied into the lambda, and allowing mutation would create race conditions). Unlike anonymous classes, `this` inside a lambda refers to the enclosing instance, and lambdas don't create a new scope for variable names. Lambdas compile to `invokedynamic`, not to separate `.class` files.

## Built-in functional interfaces (java.util.function)
| Interface | Method | Use |
|---|---|---|
| `Predicate<T>` | `boolean test(T)` | filter |
| `Function<T,R>` | `R apply(T)` | map |
| `Consumer<T>` | `void accept(T)` | forEach |
| `Supplier<T>` | `T get()` | lazy creation, `orElseGet` |
| `BiFunction<T,U,R>` | `R apply(T,U)` | merge |
| `UnaryOperator<T>` / `BinaryOperator<T>` | same type in/out | `reduce` |
Primitive variants (`IntPredicate`, `ToIntFunction`) avoid boxing. Compose them: `p1.and(p2).negate()`, `f.andThen(g)`, `f.compose(g)`.

Mark your own with `@FunctionalInterface` — the compiler then errors if a second abstract method is added. Default and static methods don't count, nor do methods from `Object` like `equals`.

## Method references
```java
list.forEach(System.out::println);      // instance method of particular object
list.stream().map(String::toUpperCase);  // instance method of arbitrary object
list.stream().map(Integer::parseInt);    // static method
Supplier<List<String>> s = ArrayList::new; // constructor
```

## Default and static methods in interfaces
Added so that interfaces like `Collection` could gain `stream()` and `forEach` without breaking every implementation. Diamond problem resolution: class methods win over interface defaults; a more specific interface wins; otherwise you must override.

## Optional
A container that may or may not hold a value — designed as a **return type** to make "no result" explicit.
```java
Optional<User> u = repo.findById(id);
String city = u.map(User::getAddress)
               .map(Address::getCity)
               .orElse("Unknown");
User user = u.orElseThrow(() -> new ResourceNotFoundException("User", id));
u.ifPresentOrElse(this::send, () -> log.info("none")); // Java 9
```
- `orElse(x)` always evaluates `x`; `orElseGet(() -> x)` evaluates lazily. Use `orElseGet` when the default is expensive (DB call).
- `Optional.of(null)` throws NPE; use `ofNullable`.
- **Don't**: use Optional for fields, method parameters, or collections (return empty list instead), or call `get()` without checking. Optional is not `Serializable`.

## Other Java 8 additions
- **New Date/Time API** (`java.time`): `LocalDate`, `LocalDateTime`, `ZonedDateTime`, `Instant`, `Duration`, `Period`, `DateTimeFormatter`. Immutable and thread-safe, unlike `Date`/`SimpleDateFormat`.
- `CompletableFuture` for async composition.
- Metaspace replaced PermGen.
- `ConcurrentHashMap` rework, `Map.merge/compute/getOrDefault`.
- `String.join`, `StringJoiner`, `Base64`.

notes.title: Streams API Deep Dive with Coding Patterns
Modern Java (11 to 21): Records, Sealed Classes, Pattern Matching, Virtual Threads
Multithreading Basics: Threads, synchronized, volatile
Concurrency Utilities: Locks, Executors, CompletableFuture, Deadlock
notes.content:
## Lock interface (java.util.concurrent.locks)
```java
private final ReentrantLock lock = new ReentrantLock(true); // fair
void transfer() {
    if (lock.tryLock(1, TimeUnit.SECONDS)) {
        try { ... } finally { lock.unlock(); }   // always unlock in finally
    }
}
```
Advantages over `synchronized`: `tryLock` with timeout, interruptible lock acquisition (`lockInterruptibly`), fairness option, multiple `Condition`s (`await/signal`). Downside: must unlock manually.
- `ReentrantReadWriteLock`: many readers OR one writer — read-heavy caches.
- `StampedLock`: optimistic reads, not reentrant.

## Synchronizers
| Tool | Purpose |
|---|---|
| `CountDownLatch(n)` | One or more threads wait until n events happen (`countDown`, `await`). Not reusable. |
| `CyclicBarrier(n)` | n threads wait for each other at a barrier, then all proceed. Reusable. |
| `Semaphore(k)` | Limit concurrent access to k permits (connection limits, rate limiting). |
| `Phaser` | Flexible, multi-phase barrier. |
| `Exchanger` | Two threads swap objects. |

## Executor framework
Creating a thread per task is expensive; thread pools reuse threads.
```java
ExecutorService pool = Executors.newFixedThreadPool(10);
Future<String> f = pool.submit(() -> fetch());
String r = f.get(2, TimeUnit.SECONDS);
pool.shutdown();                      // no new tasks, finish queued
pool.awaitTermination(30, TimeUnit.SECONDS);
```
Factory pools: `newFixedThreadPool` (unbounded `LinkedBlockingQueue`), `newCachedThreadPool` (unbounded threads, `SynchronousQueue`), `newSingleThreadExecutor`, `newScheduledThreadPool`, `newWorkStealingPool` (ForkJoin), `newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor` (21). In production, prefer a hand-configured `ThreadPoolExecutor` to avoid unbounded queues/threads causing OOM.

### ThreadPoolExecutor parameters
`corePoolSize, maximumPoolSize, keepAliveTime, workQueue, threadFactory, rejectionHandler`.
Flow: new task -> if running threads < core, new thread; else enqueue; if queue full and threads < max, new thread; else **reject**.
Rejection policies: `AbortPolicy` (default, throws), `CallerRunsPolicy` (back-pressure), `DiscardPolicy`, `DiscardOldestPolicy`.
Sizing rule of thumb: CPU-bound ~ cores + 1; I/O-bound ~ cores * (1 + wait/compute).

`submit()` returns a Future and captures exceptions inside it; `execute()` has no result and exceptions go to the thread's uncaught handler.

## CompletableFuture
`Future.get()` blocks and cannot be chained. `CompletableFuture` supports non-blocking pipelines.
```java
CompletableFuture<User> userF = CompletableFuture.supplyAsync(() -> userClient.get(id), pool);
CompletableFuture<List<Order>> ordersF = CompletableFuture.supplyAsync(() -> orderClient.list(id), pool);

CompletableFuture<Profile> profile = userF
    .thenCombine(ordersF, Profile::new)          // run both in parallel, combine
    .orTimeout(2, TimeUnit.SECONDS)
    .exceptionally(ex -> Profile.empty());       // fallback

CompletableFuture.allOf(f1, f2, f3).join();      // wait for all
CompletableFuture.anyOf(f1, f2);                 // first to complete
```
- `thenApply` (map), `thenCompose` (flatMap — chain another async call), `thenAccept` (consume), `thenCombine` (two independent futures).
- `exceptionally`, `handle` (result + exception), `whenComplete`.
- `*Async` variants run on a pool; default is `ForkJoinPool.commonPool()` — **pass your own executor** for I/O work.

## Fork/Join
Divide-and-conquer with work stealing: `RecursiveTask<T>` / `RecursiveAction`, `fork()`, `join()`. Powers parallel streams.

## Deadlock
Two or more threads wait forever for locks held by each other.
```java
// T1: lock(A) then lock(B)     T2: lock(B) then lock(A)  -> deadlock
```
**Four Coffman conditions** (all needed): mutual exclusion, hold-and-wait, no preemption, circular wait.
**Prevention:** acquire locks in a global consistent order (e.g. by account id), use `tryLock` with timeout, minimise lock scope, avoid nested locks, use higher-level concurrency utilities.
**Detection:** `jstack <pid>` or a thread dump shows "Found one Java-level deadlock"; `ThreadMXBean.findDeadlockedThreads()`.

Related: **livelock** (threads keep responding to each other but make no progress), **starvation** (a thread never gets CPU/lock — e.g. unfair locks).

notes.title: JVM Internals: Memory, Class Loading, Garbage Collection
notes.content:
## JDK vs JRE vs JVM
JVM executes bytecode; JRE = JVM + libraries; JDK = JRE + dev tools (javac, jdb, jcmd). Java is "write once, run anywhere" because `.class` bytecode runs on any platform's JVM.

## Execution pipeline
`.java` -> `javac` -> `.class` bytecode -> ClassLoader -> Bytecode verifier -> Interpreter + **JIT compiler** (C1/C2 compile hot methods to native code; tiered compilation) -> execution.

## Memory areas
| Area | Shared? | Holds |
|---|---|---|
| **Heap** | All threads | Objects, arrays, String pool. Divided into Young (Eden + 2 Survivors) and Old generation. |
| **Metaspace** (Java 8+, native memory) | All | Class metadata, method bytecode, static variable references live with the Class object on heap. Replaced PermGen. |
| **JVM Stack** | Per thread | Frames: local variables, operand stack, references. `StackOverflowError` when full. |
| **PC register** | Per thread | Current instruction address. |
| **Native method stack** | Per thread | For JNI calls. |
| Code cache | All | JIT-compiled native code. |

```java
void m() {
    int x = 5;              // primitive in stack frame
    User u = new User();    // reference 'u' in stack, object in heap
}
```

## Class loading
Phases: **Loading** -> **Linking** (verify, prepare default static values, resolve) -> **Initialization** (static blocks, static field initialisers run).
ClassLoader hierarchy: **Bootstrap** (core `java.*`), **Platform** (formerly Extension), **Application/System** (classpath). Custom loaders are used by app servers and Spring Boot's fat-jar launcher.
**Parent delegation model:** a loader first asks its parent; only if the parent can't find the class does it load itself. This prevents someone from replacing `java.lang.String` with a malicious copy, and avoids duplicate loading.
A class is identified by (fully-qualified name + its class loader).

## Garbage collection basics
- An object is eligible when it is unreachable from **GC roots** (local variables on stacks, static fields, active threads, JNI refs). Reference counting is not used, so cycles are collected.
- **Generational hypothesis:** most objects die young.
  - New objects go to **Eden**. A **Minor GC** copies live objects to a Survivor space; after surviving N cycles (tenuring threshold, default up to 15) they are promoted to **Old gen**.
  - **Major/Full GC** cleans the old generation — slower, longer pauses.
- Basic algorithm: **mark** live objects, **sweep** dead ones, **compact** to remove fragmentation. Young gen uses copying.
- "Stop-the-world" pauses freeze application threads.

## Collectors
| GC | Notes |
|---|---|
| Serial | Single thread; small heaps/clients. |
| Parallel | Multi-threaded, throughput-focused (default in Java 8). |
| CMS | Concurrent mark-sweep; deprecated (9) and removed (14). |
| **G1** (default since Java 9) | Heap divided into equal-sized **regions**; collects regions with most garbage first ("Garbage First"); target pause via `-XX:MaxGCPauseMillis=200`; concurrent marking; mixed collections; compacts incrementally. Good balance for 4GB+ heaps. |
| **ZGC** | Ultra-low pause (<1ms typically), scales to TB heaps, concurrent compaction using coloured pointers and load barriers. Generational from Java 21 (`-XX:+UseZGC -XX:+ZGenerational`; default generational in 23). |
| Shenandoah | Low-pause, concurrent compaction (Red Hat). |
| Epsilon | No-op GC for testing. |

## Reference types
Strong (normal), **Soft** (cleared only under memory pressure — caches), **Weak** (cleared at next GC — `WeakHashMap`), **Phantom** (post-mortem cleanup, `Cleaner`).

## Important flags & tools
`-Xms` initial heap, `-Xmx` max heap, `-Xss` thread stack size, `-XX:MaxMetaspaceSize`, `-XX:+HeapDumpOnOutOfMemoryError`.
Tools: `jps`, `jstack` (thread dump), `jmap`/`jcmd GC.heap_dump` (heap dump), `jstat` (GC stats), VisualVM, JFR + JMC, Eclipse MAT for leak analysis.

## Memory leaks in Java
Even with GC, leaks happen when objects stay reachable: static collections that grow, unbounded caches, unremoved listeners, `ThreadLocal` in pools, unclosed resources, inner classes holding outer references. Diagnose with heap dumps and the dominator tree.

notes.title: Serialization, Cloning and Misc Core Topics
notes.content:
## Serialization
Converting an object to a byte stream (to save to disk/send over network) and back (deserialization).
```java
class User implements Serializable {
    private static final long serialVersionUID = 1L;
    private String name;
    private transient String password;   // not serialized -> null after deserialization
}
try (var out = new ObjectOutputStream(new FileOutputStream("u.ser"))) { out.writeObject(user); }
try (var in = new ObjectInputStream(new FileInputStream("u.ser"))) { User u = (User) in.readObject(); }
```
- `Serializable` is a **marker interface** (no methods).
- `serialVersionUID` — version check. If not declared, the JVM computes one from the class structure; any change (adding a field) changes it and deserialization throws `InvalidClassException`. Always declare it.
- `transient` and `static` fields are not serialized.
- If a parent class is not Serializable, it must have a no-arg constructor; its fields get re-initialised by that constructor.
- All referenced objects must be Serializable, otherwise `NotSerializableException`.
- Customise with `private void writeObject/readObject`, or `Externalizable` (`writeExternal/readExternal`, needs public no-arg constructor, full control, faster).
- `readResolve()` preserves singletons during deserialization.
- **Security:** Java native deserialization of untrusted data is a well-known RCE vector. Modern systems use JSON (Jackson), Protobuf, or Avro. Use deserialization filters (`ObjectInputFilter`) if you must.

## Jackson (the serialization you actually use in Spring)
```java
ObjectMapper om = new ObjectMapper();
String json = om.writeValueAsString(dto);
UserDto dto = om.readValue(json, UserDto.class);
List<UserDto> list = om.readValue(json, new TypeReference<List<UserDto>>() {});
```
Annotations: `@JsonIgnore`, `@JsonProperty`, `@JsonFormat`, `@JsonInclude(NON_NULL)`, `@JsonIgnoreProperties(ignoreUnknown = true)`. Bidirectional JPA relations need `@JsonManagedReference/@JsonBackReference` or DTOs to avoid infinite recursion.

## Pass by value
Java is **always pass-by-value**. For objects, the value passed is a copy of the reference. So a method can mutate the object's fields, but reassigning the parameter does not affect the caller.
```java
void change(StringBuilder sb) { sb.append("x"); sb = new StringBuilder("new"); }
```
Caller sees the appended "x" but not "new".

## Wrapper classes and autoboxing
```java
Integer a = 127, b = 127;  a == b  // true  (Integer cache -128..127)
Integer c = 128, d = 128;  c == d  // false (different objects)
```
Always compare wrappers with `equals`. Unboxing a null `Integer` throws NPE.

## Static vs instance initialisation order
1. Static blocks/fields of parent, then child (once, at class load).
2. On `new`: parent instance blocks + constructor, then child instance blocks + constructor.

## Inner classes
- Static nested class — no reference to outer instance (preferred).
- Inner (non-static) — holds implicit outer reference (can cause leaks).
- Local and anonymous classes. Lambdas replaced most anonymous class uses.

## Reflection
`Class.forName`, `getDeclaredMethods`, `setAccessible(true)`, `method.invoke`. Used by Spring (DI, annotations), Hibernate, Jackson, JUnit. Slower and bypasses encapsulation. Annotations with `@Retention(RUNTIME)` are readable by reflection.

## Immutable collections & defensive copies
`List.of`, `List.copyOf`, `Collections.unmodifiableList` (view — the backing list can still change).

## final, finally, finalize
`final` keyword (constant/no override/no inherit); `finally` block always executes; `finalize()` was a GC callback — deprecated for removal (Java 9/18), use `try-with-resources` or `Cleaner`.

## Enum
Type-safe constants; can have fields, constructors (private), methods, and implement interfaces. Enum singletons are serialization- and reflection-safe. `EnumMap`/`EnumSet` are highly efficient.

qa.q: What are the four pillars of OOP? Explain each with a Java example.
qa.a:
- **Encapsulation**: hide state behind methods that enforce rules. `BankAccount` keeps `balance` private and validates in `deposit()`.
- **Abstraction**: expose *what*, hide *how*. A `PaymentGateway` interface with `charge()`; callers don't know if Razorpay or Stripe is used.
- **Inheritance**: reuse via "is-a". `SavingsAccount extends Account`. Java allows one superclass but many interfaces.
- **Polymorphism**: one reference type, many behaviours. Overloading is compile-time; overriding is runtime (dynamic dispatch).

```java
PaymentGateway g = new RazorpayGateway();
g.charge(order);   // runtime decides which implementation runs
```
Tie it to your project: e.g. multiple `NotificationSender` beans injected as a list and chosen by type.

qa.q: What is the difference between an abstract class and an interface in Java 8+?
qa.a:
| Abstract class | Interface |
|---|---|
| Can have instance fields and constructors | Only `public static final` constants, no constructors |
| Any access modifiers on methods | Abstract, `default`, `static`, `private` (Java 9) methods |
| Single inheritance | A class can implement many |
| Models "is-a" with shared state/code | Models a capability/contract ("can-do") |

Use an abstract class when related classes share state and partial implementation (template method pattern). Use an interface to define a contract that unrelated classes can implement (`Comparable`, `Runnable`), and for DI in Spring. Default methods were added so existing interfaces (like `Collection`) could evolve without breaking implementations. If two interfaces have the same default method, the class must override and pick with `A.super.m()`.

qa.q: Method overloading vs overriding — what are the rules?
qa.a:
**Overloading** (compile-time polymorphism): same method name, different parameter list (number/type/order) in the same class. Return type alone can't differ.

**Overriding** (runtime polymorphism): subclass redefines a parent method with the same signature.
Rules for overriding:
- Return type same or covariant (subtype).
- Access can't be narrower (`protected` -> `public` allowed).
- Can't throw new or broader **checked** exceptions.
- `final`, `static` and `private` methods can't be overridden. Static methods with the same signature are **hidden**, chosen by reference type.
- Use `@Override` to let the compiler catch mistakes.

```java
class A { static void s(){print("A");} void i(){print("A");} }
class B extends A { static void s(){print("B");} void i(){print("B");} }
A x = new B(); x.s(); /* A */ x.i(); /* B */
```

qa.q: Can we override a static or private method? Can we overload main()?
qa.a:
- **Static methods**: No. Declaring the same static method in a subclass *hides* the parent's; the call is resolved by the reference type at compile time, not the object type.
- **Private methods**: No. They're not visible to subclasses; a same-named method in the subclass is an unrelated new method.
- **main()**: Yes, it can be overloaded (`main(int x)`), but the JVM only calls `public static void main(String[] args)` as the entry point. It can't be overridden in the polymorphic sense because it's static.
- **Constructors**: can be overloaded, never overridden (not inherited).

qa.q: Why is String immutable in Java?
qa.a:
`String` is `final` and its internal `byte[]` is `private final` with no mutators. Reasons:
1. **String pool** — literals are shared between references; mutation would affect everyone.
2. **Security** — DB URLs, file paths, class names, usernames can't be altered after validation.
3. **Thread safety** — immutable objects need no synchronization.
4. **Hash caching** — `hashCode` is computed once and cached, making Strings fast and safe `HashMap` keys.
5. **Class loading** relies on string names that must not change.

The trade-off is that repeated modification creates garbage; use `StringBuilder` for that.

qa.q: How many objects are created by `String s = new String("hello")`? What's the String pool?
qa.a:
**One or two.** The literal `"hello"` is placed in the String pool if not already present (one object), and `new` always creates a separate object on the heap (second object). `s` refers to the heap object.

The **String pool** is a special area (in the heap since Java 7) where string literals are interned so identical literals share one object.
```java
String a = "hello", b = "hello";
String c = new String("hello");
a == b;            // true
a == c;            // false
a == c.intern();   // true - intern returns pooled copy
a.equals(c);       // true
```
Always use `equals()` for content comparison.

qa.q: String vs StringBuilder vs StringBuffer?
qa.a:
| | String | StringBuilder | StringBuffer |
|---|---|---|---|
| Mutability | Immutable | Mutable | Mutable |
| Thread safety | Safe (immutable) | Not synchronized | Synchronized methods |
| Performance | Each change = new object | Fastest | Slower due to locking |
| Since | 1.0 | 1.5 | 1.0 |

Use `String` for fixed values, `StringBuilder` for building strings in a loop (local variable — no sharing), and `StringBuffer` rarely (legacy). Concatenation with `+` in a loop is O(n^2) because each iteration copies.
```java
StringBuilder sb = new StringBuilder();
for (String w : words) sb.append(w).append(',');
```

qa.q: What is the equals() and hashCode() contract? What happens if you override only equals()?
qa.a:
Contract: if `a.equals(b)` then `a.hashCode() == b.hashCode()`. Equal hash codes do not imply equality. `equals` must be reflexive, symmetric, transitive, consistent, and false for null.

If you override only `equals`, two logically equal objects will usually have different identity hash codes. Hash-based collections look up the **bucket by hashCode first**, so:
```java
Set<Emp> s = new HashSet<>();
s.add(new Emp(1));
s.contains(new Emp(1)); // false
s.add(new Emp(1));      // duplicate stored
```
Fix: override both, using the same fields, e.g. `Objects.hash(id, email)`. Records and Lombok `@EqualsAndHashCode` generate them consistently.

qa.q: Explain the internal working of HashMap in Java 8.
qa.a:
- Backed by `Node<K,V>[] table` (default capacity 16, load factor 0.75).
- **put**: compute `hash = h ^ (h >>> 16)` of `key.hashCode()`; index = `(n-1) & hash`. If bucket empty, insert. Else traverse: if a node's key `equals` the new key, replace the value; otherwise append to the list.
- **Treeification**: when a bucket exceeds 8 nodes and capacity >= 64, it becomes a red-black tree (O(log n) lookups); it untreeifies at 6. If capacity < 64 it resizes instead.
- **Resize**: when size > capacity x load factor (12 by default), capacity doubles; each node either stays at index `i` or moves to `i + oldCap`.
- **get**: same hash/index, then `equals` within the bucket.
- Allows one null key (bucket 0) and many null values. Not thread-safe.

Average O(1) get/put; worst case O(log n) with tree bins.

qa.q: Why is HashMap capacity always a power of two? What is the load factor?
qa.a:
With capacity `n` a power of two, `(n - 1) & hash` is equivalent to `hash % n` but much faster (a bitwise AND), and it uses all low bits evenly. That's also why HashMap spreads the hash with `h ^ (h >>> 16)` — so high bits influence the index. If you pass `new HashMap<>(100)`, it rounds up to 128.

The **load factor** (default 0.75) controls when to resize: threshold = capacity x load factor. 0.75 is a trade-off — lower means fewer collisions but more memory; higher saves memory but increases collisions. If you know the expected size, pre-size to avoid repeated resizing: `new HashMap<>((int)(expected / 0.75f) + 1)` or Java 19's `HashMap.newHashMap(expected)`.

qa.q: What is a hash collision and how does HashMap handle it?
qa.a:
A collision happens when two different keys map to the same bucket index (either the same hashCode or different hashCodes that produce the same index). HashMap uses **separate chaining**: entries in the same bucket are stored as a linked list, and from Java 8 the list converts to a **red-black tree** once it exceeds 8 nodes (with table size >= 64). Lookups in the bucket compare hash first, then `equals()`.

A poor `hashCode()` (e.g. returning a constant) puts everything in one bucket, degrading performance to O(n) (or O(log n) with treeification if keys are `Comparable`). Good hashCode implementations use all significant fields, e.g. `Objects.hash(...)`.

qa.q: HashMap vs Hashtable vs ConcurrentHashMap vs synchronizedMap?
qa.a:
| | HashMap | Hashtable | synchronizedMap | ConcurrentHashMap |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Thread-safe | No | Yes | Yes | Yes |
| Locking | None | Whole table (every method synchronized) | Whole map (wrapper mutex) | Bucket-level (CAS + synchronized on bin head), lock-free reads |
| Null key/values | 1 null key, null values | None | Depends on backing map | None |
| Iterator | Fail-fast | Fail-fast (enumerator not) | Fail-fast (must sync manually) | Weakly consistent |
| Performance | Best single-threaded | Poor | Poor under contention | Excellent under contention |

Use HashMap for single-thread/local use, ConcurrentHashMap for shared maps. Hashtable is legacy.

qa.q: How does ConcurrentHashMap work internally in Java 8? Why doesn't it allow null?
qa.a:
Java 7 used 16 lock-striped segments. Java 8+ removed segments:
- Same array-of-bins structure as HashMap with tree bins.
- **Reads** are lock-free: node values and next pointers are `volatile`.
- **Writes to an empty bin** use **CAS**.
- **Writes to a non-empty bin** `synchronized` on the bin's first node — only that bucket is locked.
- **Resizing** is done cooperatively by multiple threads using `ForwardingNode` markers.
- `size()` uses striped counter cells (like `LongAdder`).

**No nulls** because in concurrent code `get(k) == null` would be ambiguous (absent vs mapped to null), and checking `containsKey` afterwards isn't atomic. Use `computeIfAbsent`, `merge`, `putIfAbsent` for atomic compound actions.

qa.q: ArrayList vs LinkedList — when would you use each?
qa.a:
- **ArrayList**: dynamic array. O(1) random access, amortised O(1) append, O(n) insert/delete in the middle (shifting). Compact and CPU-cache friendly. Grows by 1.5x.
- **LinkedList**: doubly linked list. O(n) access by index, O(1) insert/remove at ends or at a known iterator position, but finding the position is O(n). Each node has extra overhead (two pointers + object header).

In practice ArrayList is faster for almost all workloads, even many middle insertions, due to cache locality. Use `ArrayDeque` for queue/stack operations instead of LinkedList. LinkedList is mainly useful when you frequently remove/insert via an `Iterator`/`ListIterator` while traversing.

qa.q: How does ArrayList grow internally?
qa.a:
ArrayList holds an `Object[] elementData`. `new ArrayList<>()` starts with a shared empty array; the first `add` allocates capacity **10**. When full, `grow()` creates a new array of size `old + (old >> 1)` (i.e. **1.5x**) and copies elements with `Arrays.copyOf` (System.arraycopy). That's why append is amortised O(1).

Tips: if you know the size, use `new ArrayList<>(n)` or `ensureCapacity(n)` to avoid repeated copying; `trimToSize()` releases unused capacity. Removing elements does not shrink the array automatically.

qa.q: Fail-fast vs fail-safe iterators? How do you avoid ConcurrentModificationException?
qa.a:
**Fail-fast** iterators (ArrayList, HashMap, HashSet) record `modCount` when created. If the collection is structurally modified other than through the iterator, the next `next()` throws `ConcurrentModificationException`. It's best-effort, not guaranteed.

**Fail-safe / weakly consistent** iterators (CopyOnWriteArrayList, ConcurrentHashMap) work on a snapshot or tolerate concurrent changes and never throw CME.

Avoiding CME while removing:
```java
list.removeIf(x -> x < 0);                         // best
Iterator<Integer> it = list.iterator();
while (it.hasNext()) if (it.next() < 0) it.remove(); // iterator's own remove
```
Don't call `list.remove()` inside a for-each loop.

qa.q: HashSet vs LinkedHashSet vs TreeSet? How does HashSet ensure uniqueness?
qa.a:
- **HashSet**: backed by a `HashMap` (elements are keys, value is a dummy `PRESENT` object). No order, O(1) ops, allows one null.
- **LinkedHashSet**: backed by LinkedHashMap — keeps **insertion order**.
- **TreeSet**: backed by TreeMap (red-black tree) — **sorted** order, O(log n), uses `compareTo`/Comparator (not equals) for uniqueness, no null with natural ordering.

Uniqueness in HashSet comes from `HashMap.put`: `add(e)` returns false if a key with the same `hashCode` and `equals` already exists. So custom objects need correct equals/hashCode.

qa.q: How does TreeMap work, and when would you use it over HashMap?
qa.a:
TreeMap is a **red-black tree** (self-balancing BST) that keeps keys sorted by natural order or a supplied Comparator. `get/put/remove` are O(log n). It offers navigation APIs: `firstKey`, `lastKey`, `floorKey`, `ceilingKey`, `headMap`, `tailMap`, `subMap`, `descendingMap`.

Use it when you need sorted keys or range queries: leaderboards, time-based buckets, finding the nearest price slab, scheduling.
```java
TreeMap<Integer, String> slabs = new TreeMap<>(Map.of(0,"NIL", 250000,"5%", 500000,"20%"));
slabs.floorEntry(320000).getValue(); // "5%"
```
It doesn't permit null keys with natural ordering, and isn't thread-safe (use `ConcurrentSkipListMap`).

qa.q: How would you implement an LRU cache in Java?
Comparable vs Comparator?
qa.a:
- `Comparable<T>` is implemented by the class itself: `int compareTo(T o)` — the **natural ordering** (one per class). Used by `Collections.sort(list)`, TreeMap keys.
- `Comparator<T>` is an external strategy: `int compare(T a, T b)` — you can define many orderings without modifying the class.

```java
emps.sort(Comparator.comparing(Emp::dept)
        .thenComparing(Emp::salary, Comparator.reverseOrder())
        .thenComparing(Emp::name));
```
Keep `compareTo` consistent with `equals`, because sorted collections treat `compareTo == 0` as duplicate. Avoid `a - b` style comparisons (overflow); use `Integer.compare`.

qa.q: What are generics and what is type erasure?
qa.a:
Generics provide compile-time type safety and eliminate casts: `List<String>` only accepts Strings.

**Type erasure**: generic type info is removed by the compiler. Type parameters are replaced with their bound (or `Object`), casts are inserted, and bridge methods are generated. At runtime `List<String>` and `List<Integer>` are both just `ArrayList`.

Consequences:
- Can't do `new T()`, `new T[]`, `instanceof List<String>`.
- Can't overload methods differing only in generic type (`f(List<String>)` vs `f(List<Integer>)`).
- Can't use primitives as type arguments.
- Static fields can't be of type `T`.
It was chosen for backward compatibility with pre-Java-5 code. Workarounds: pass `Class<T>` tokens or `TypeReference`.

qa.q: Explain wildcards `? extends` and `? super` (PECS).
qa.a:
- `List<? extends Number>`: any list of Number or subtype. You can **read** elements as `Number`, but can't add (compiler can't know the exact type). It's a **producer**.
- `List<? super Integer>`: list of Integer or a supertype. You can **add** Integers, but reads return `Object`. It's a **consumer**.

**PECS** — Producer Extends, Consumer Super:
```java
static double sum(List<? extends Number> nums) { double s=0; for (Number n: nums) s+=n.doubleValue(); return s; }
static void fill(List<? super Integer> out) { out.add(1); out.add(2); }
```
`Collections.copy(List<? super T> dest, List<? extends T> src)` is the classic JDK example. Generics are invariant: `List<Integer>` is not a `List<Number>`.

qa.q: Checked vs unchecked exceptions? When do you use each?
qa.a:
- **Checked** (subclasses of `Exception` but not `RuntimeException`): compiler forces catch or `throws`. Examples: `IOException`, `SQLException`. Use for recoverable conditions outside your control.
- **Unchecked** (`RuntimeException` and subclasses): no compile-time enforcement. Examples: `NullPointerException`, `IllegalArgumentException`. Represent programming errors or business rule violations.
- **Errors** (`OutOfMemoryError`, `StackOverflowError`): serious JVM problems; don't catch.

Modern Spring code mostly uses unchecked custom exceptions (e.g. `ResourceNotFoundException`) handled centrally by `@RestControllerAdvice`. Note: `@Transactional` rolls back by default only for unchecked exceptions and Errors, not checked ones (unless `rollbackFor` is set).

qa.q: Does finally always execute? What happens with return in try and finally?
What is try-with-resources and what are suppressed exceptions?
How do you create a custom exception, and how do you handle exceptions globally in a Spring Boot app?
What is a functional interface? Name the important ones in java.util.function.
qa.a:
An interface with exactly **one abstract method** (SAM); it can be the target of a lambda or method reference. `@FunctionalInterface` makes the compiler enforce this. Default/static methods and `Object` methods don't count.

| Interface | Abstract method |
|---|---|
| `Predicate<T>` | `boolean test(T)` |
| `Function<T,R>` | `R apply(T)` |
| `Consumer<T>` | `void accept(T)` |
| `Supplier<T>` | `T get()` |
| `BiFunction<T,U,R>` | `R apply(T,U)` |
| `UnaryOperator<T>`, `BinaryOperator<T>` | same-type operations |

Older examples: `Runnable`, `Callable`, `Comparator`. Composition: `Predicate.and/or/negate`, `Function.andThen/compose`.

qa.q: Why must local variables used in a lambda be effectively final?
qa.a:
A lambda captures the **value** of a local variable, not the variable itself (locals live on the stack frame, which may be gone when the lambda runs later, possibly on another thread). If mutation were allowed, the lambda's copy and the original could diverge and you'd get race conditions. So Java requires captured locals to be final or effectively final (never reassigned).

```java
int count = 0;
list.forEach(x -> count++);         // compile error
AtomicInteger c = new AtomicInteger();
list.forEach(x -> c.incrementAndGet()); // ok - reference is final, object mutable
```
Instance and static fields can be modified because they live on the heap (accessed via `this`). Better: use `stream().count()` instead of mutating.

qa.q: What is Optional? What is the difference between orElse and orElseGet?
qa.a:
`Optional<T>` is a container that may hold a value, intended as a **method return type** to signal "may be absent" and avoid null checks/NPEs.

```java
String name = repo.findById(id).map(User::getName).orElse("guest");
User u = repo.findById(id).orElseThrow(() -> new NotFoundException(id));
```
- `orElse(x)`: `x` is **always evaluated**, even if a value is present.
- `orElseGet(supplier)`: supplier runs **only** when empty — use it for expensive defaults (DB/API calls, object creation).

Best practices: don't use Optional for fields, parameters or collections; never call `get()` without a check (prefer `orElseThrow()`); use `Optional.ofNullable` for possibly-null values.

qa.q: map() vs flatMap() in streams?
qa.a:
- `map` transforms each element to exactly one element: `Stream<T> -> Stream<R>`.
- `flatMap` transforms each element to a **stream** and flattens them into one: one-to-many.

```java
List<String> sentences = List.of("hello world", "java streams");
sentences.stream().map(s -> s.split(" "));                 // Stream<String[]>
sentences.stream().flatMap(s -> Arrays.stream(s.split(" ")))
         .toList();                                          // [hello, world, java, streams]

orders.stream().flatMap(o -> o.getItems().stream())          // all items across orders
      .mapToDouble(Item::price).sum();
```
Same idea for Optional: `Optional.flatMap` avoids `Optional<Optional<T>>`.

qa.q: Intermediate vs terminal operations; what is lazy evaluation in streams?
qa.a:
- **Intermediate** ops (`filter`, `map`, `sorted`, `distinct`, `limit`) return a new Stream and are **lazy** — they only build the pipeline.
- **Terminal** ops (`collect`, `forEach`, `reduce`, `count`, `findFirst`, `anyMatch`) trigger processing and close the stream.

Elements flow one at a time through the whole pipeline (vertical processing), so short-circuiting ops stop early:
```java
Stream.of(1,2,3,4,5)
    .filter(x -> { System.out.println("f" + x); return x % 2 == 0; })
    .findFirst();   // prints f1, f2 only
```
A stream can be consumed only once; reusing throws `IllegalStateException`. Stateful ops like `sorted` must consume all input before emitting.

qa.q: Using streams, group employees by department and count them; also find the average salary per department.
Find the second highest salary using Java streams.
qa.a:
```java
Optional<Double> second = emps.stream()
    .map(Emp::salary)
    .distinct()                              // handle duplicate top salaries
    .sorted(Comparator.reverseOrder())
    .skip(1)
    .findFirst();

// the employee(s) earning it
List<Emp> who = second.map(s -> emps.stream().filter(e -> e.salary() == s).toList())
                      .orElse(List.of());
// Nth highest: skip(n - 1)
```
For a plain `int[]`: `Arrays.stream(a).boxed().distinct().sorted(Comparator.reverseOrder()).skip(1).findFirst()`.
Interviewers often follow up: complexity is O(n log n) due to sorting; an O(n) approach tracks `first` and `second` in a single loop.

qa.q: Find duplicate elements in a list using streams.
Find the first non-repeating character in a string using streams.
qa.a:
```java
String s = "swiss";
Character result = s.chars()
    .mapToObj(c -> (char) c)
    .collect(Collectors.groupingBy(Function.identity(),
             LinkedHashMap::new,          // preserve encounter order
             Collectors.counting()))
    .entrySet().stream()
    .filter(e -> e.getValue() == 1)
    .map(Map.Entry::getKey)
    .findFirst()
    .orElse(null);   // 'w'
```
The key is `LinkedHashMap::new` — a plain HashMap loses order. First *repeating* character: change the filter to `> 1`. Non-stream O(n): `int[256]` counts then a second pass over the string.

qa.q: Stream coding: highest-paid employee in each department, and names of employees grouped by department.
Stream coding: partition numbers into even/odd, sum of squares of odd numbers, and sort a map by value.
qa.a:
```java
Map<Boolean, List<Integer>> parts = nums.stream()
    .collect(Collectors.partitioningBy(n -> n % 2 == 0));   // true -> evens

int sumSqOdd = nums.stream().filter(n -> n % 2 != 0).mapToInt(n -> n * n).sum();

LinkedHashMap<String, Integer> byValueDesc = map.entrySet().stream()
    .sorted(Map.Entry.<String, Integer>comparingByValue().reversed())
    .collect(Collectors.toMap(Map.Entry::getKey, Map.Entry::getValue,
             (a, b) -> a, LinkedHashMap::new));   // keep sorted order

// Count words, top 3 most frequent
Arrays.stream(text.toLowerCase().split("\\W+"))
    .collect(Collectors.groupingBy(w -> w, Collectors.counting()))
    .entrySet().stream()
    .sorted(Map.Entry.<String, Long>comparingByValue().reversed())
    .limit(3).map(Map.Entry::getKey).toList();
```

qa.q: Stream coding: join list of strings, find max/min, check palindromes, and convert a List to a Map.
What is the difference between Collectors.toList() and Stream.toList()?
qa.a:
- `Collectors.toList()` (Java 8): returns a list with no guarantees on type/mutability; in practice a mutable `ArrayList`, and it accepts nulls.
- `Stream.toList()` (Java 16): returns an **unmodifiable** list (calling `add` throws `UnsupportedOperationException`), allows nulls, and is slightly more efficient.
- `Collectors.toUnmodifiableList()` (Java 10): unmodifiable and **rejects nulls**.

Choose `toList()` for read-only results (most cases) and `Collectors.toCollection(ArrayList::new)` when the caller must modify the list.

qa.q: When should you use parallel streams? What are the pitfalls?
qa.a:
`parallelStream()` splits data with a `Spliterator` and processes chunks on the common `ForkJoinPool` (parallelism = cores - 1).

Use when: large data sets (tens of thousands+), CPU-intensive, stateless and independent operations, easily-splittable sources (arrays, ArrayList, ranges).

Pitfalls:
- Overhead makes small collections slower.
- Shared common pool — blocking I/O in one parallel stream starves others (bad in web servers).
- Side effects/shared mutable state cause race conditions.
- Ordering costs: `findFirst`, `forEachOrdered`, `limit` on ordered streams are expensive; use `findAny` / `unordered()`.
- LinkedList and `Stream.iterate` split poorly.
Always measure before using.

qa.q: What are records in Java? Can a record be a JPA entity?
What are sealed classes and how do they combine with pattern matching for switch?
What are virtual threads in Java 21? How are they different from platform threads?
What new features came in Java 11, 17 and 21 that you have used or know about?
qa.a:
**Java 11**: `var` in lambdas, `String.isBlank/strip/lines/repeat`, `Files.readString/writeString`, standard `HttpClient`, `Optional.isEmpty`, run single-file programs.

**Java 17**: records, sealed classes, pattern matching for `instanceof`, switch expressions, text blocks, helpful NPE messages, strong encapsulation of JDK internals.

**Java 21**: virtual threads, pattern matching for switch, record patterns, sequenced collections (`getFirst/getLast/reversed`), generational ZGC.

Spring Boot 3 requires Java 17+, so most product companies run 17 or 21 now. Mention which you actually used (e.g. "records for DTOs and switch expressions in our order-status mapper").

qa.q: What is the difference between a process and a thread? Explain the thread lifecycle.
qa.a:
A **process** is an independent program with its own memory space; a **thread** is a unit of execution within a process that shares the heap with other threads but has its own stack and PC. Threads are cheaper to create and switch, but shared memory requires synchronization.

Thread states (`Thread.State`):
1. **NEW** — created, `start()` not called.
2. **RUNNABLE** — running or ready to run.
3. **BLOCKED** — waiting to enter a `synchronized` block held by another thread.
4. **WAITING** — `wait()`, `join()`, `LockSupport.park()` without timeout.
5. **TIMED_WAITING** — `sleep(ms)`, `wait(ms)`, `join(ms)`.
6. **TERMINATED** — `run()` finished.

qa.q: What is the difference between calling start() and run() on a thread?
qa.a:
`start()` asks the JVM to create a new thread with its own call stack, moves it to RUNNABLE, and that new thread invokes `run()`. Calling `run()` directly is just a normal method call on the **current** thread — no concurrency.
```java
Thread t = new Thread(() -> System.out.println(Thread.currentThread().getName()));
t.run();   // prints "main"
t.start(); // prints "Thread-0"
```
Calling `start()` twice on the same Thread throws `IllegalThreadStateException`.

qa.q: Runnable vs Callable? execute() vs submit()?
qa.a:
- `Runnable.run()` returns nothing and can't throw checked exceptions.
- `Callable<V>.call()` returns a value and can throw checked exceptions.

`ExecutorService`:
- `execute(Runnable)` — fire-and-forget; an exception goes to the thread's `UncaughtExceptionHandler` (and the worker thread dies and is replaced).
- `submit(Runnable/Callable)` — returns a `Future`; exceptions are captured inside it and rethrown as `ExecutionException` on `future.get()`. If you never call `get()`, the exception is silently lost — a common production bug.
```java
Future<Integer> f = pool.submit(() -> compute());
try { f.get(1, TimeUnit.SECONDS); } catch (ExecutionException e) { log.error("failed", e.getCause()); }
```

qa.q: Difference between wait() and sleep()?
qa.a:
| wait() | sleep() |
|---|---|
| Method of `Object` | Static method of `Thread` |
| **Releases** the monitor lock | **Keeps** any locks held |
| Must be called inside `synchronized` (else `IllegalMonitorStateException`) | Can be called anywhere |
| Woken by `notify/notifyAll`, timeout, or interrupt | Wakes after timeout or interrupt |
| Used for inter-thread communication | Used to pause execution |

Always call `wait()` in a loop that re-checks the condition because of spurious wakeups:
```java
synchronized (lock) { while (!ready) lock.wait(); }
```

qa.q: What does synchronized do? Method vs block synchronization?
What is volatile? Is volatile enough to make count++ thread-safe?
qa.a:
`volatile` guarantees **visibility** (every read sees the latest write, values aren't cached in CPU registers/caches) and **ordering** (prevents reordering around the variable, establishing happens-before). It does **not** provide atomicity.

`count++` is three steps — read, add, write — so two threads can read the same value and lose an update even if `count` is volatile. Fix with `AtomicInteger.incrementAndGet()`, `LongAdder`, or `synchronized`.

Good uses of volatile: a shutdown flag read by a worker loop; publishing an immutable object reference; double-checked locking singletons.

qa.q: What are atomic classes and how does CAS work?
qa.a:
`java.util.concurrent.atomic` (`AtomicInteger`, `AtomicLong`, `AtomicBoolean`, `AtomicReference`, `LongAdder`) provides lock-free thread-safe operations built on **Compare-And-Swap** — a CPU instruction that atomically sets a variable to a new value *only if* it still holds the expected value.
```java
// conceptually, incrementAndGet:
do { old = value; next = old + 1; } while (!compareAndSet(old, next));
```
No blocking, no context switches; under heavy contention spins retry. `LongAdder` reduces contention by spreading updates across cells and summing on read — better for high-write counters (metrics).

The **ABA problem** (value changes A->B->A unnoticed) is solved with `AtomicStampedReference`.

qa.q: ReentrantLock vs synchronized?
qa.a:
Both provide mutual exclusion, reentrancy and visibility. `ReentrantLock` adds:
- `tryLock()` / `tryLock(timeout)` — avoid waiting forever (deadlock avoidance).
- `lockInterruptibly()` — waiting can be interrupted.
- **Fairness** option (longest waiting thread gets the lock).
- Multiple `Condition` objects (`await/signal`) vs a single wait-set.
- Query methods (`isLocked`, `getQueueLength`).

Downside: you must `unlock()` in `finally`, otherwise the lock leaks.
```java
lock.lock();
try { balance -= amt; } finally { lock.unlock(); }
```
Use `synchronized` for simple cases (less error-prone); use `ReentrantLock` when you need timeouts, fairness, or conditions — and with virtual threads on Java 21. `ReadWriteLock` allows concurrent readers.

qa.q: What is a deadlock? How do you detect and prevent it?
Write a program where two threads print odd and even numbers alternately.
Implement producer-consumer in Java.
Explain the Executor framework and ThreadPoolExecutor parameters. Why avoid Executors.newFixedThreadPool in production?
qa.a:
Executors decouple task submission from thread management and reuse threads. `ThreadPoolExecutor(core, max, keepAlive, unit, workQueue, threadFactory, rejectedHandler)`:
1. Threads < core -> create a new thread.
2. Else -> put the task in the queue.
3. Queue full and threads < max -> create a thread.
4. Else -> rejection policy (`AbortPolicy` default, `CallerRunsPolicy`, `DiscardPolicy`, `DiscardOldestPolicy`).

`newFixedThreadPool` uses an **unbounded** `LinkedBlockingQueue` — under load, tasks pile up until OutOfMemoryError (and `max` is never used). `newCachedThreadPool` allows unbounded threads. Prefer:
```java
new ThreadPoolExecutor(8, 16, 60, TimeUnit.SECONDS,
    new ArrayBlockingQueue<>(500),
    new ThreadFactoryBuilder().setNameFormat("order-%d").build(), // Guava, or custom
    new ThreadPoolExecutor.CallerRunsPolicy());
```
Name threads, bound queues, and always `shutdown()` gracefully.

qa.q: What is CompletableFuture? How do you call two services in parallel and combine results?
CountDownLatch vs CyclicBarrier vs Semaphore?
qa.a:
- **CountDownLatch(n)**: one or more threads `await()` until `countDown()` has been called n times. One-shot, not reusable. Example: main thread waits until 3 services are warmed up.
- **CyclicBarrier(n)**: n threads call `await()` and all block until the last arrives, then proceed together (optional barrier action). **Reusable**. Example: parallel simulation steps.
- **Semaphore(k)**: maintains k permits; `acquire()` blocks when none left, `release()` returns one. Limits concurrency, e.g. max 10 concurrent calls to a third-party API.
```java
Semaphore s = new Semaphore(10);
s.acquire(); try { callApi(); } finally { s.release(); }
```

qa.q: What is ThreadLocal and what problems can it cause?
qa.a:
`ThreadLocal<T>` gives each thread its own independent copy of a variable.
```java
private static final ThreadLocal<String> TENANT = new ThreadLocal<>();
TENANT.set("acme"); ... TENANT.get(); ... TENANT.remove();
```
Uses: request/user context, MDC logging, Spring's `SecurityContextHolder` and transaction synchronization, non-thread-safe objects like `SimpleDateFormat`.

Problems:
- **Memory leaks / data bleed in thread pools**: pooled threads live forever, so values stay (and the next request may see the previous user's data). Always `remove()` in a `finally` / filter.
- Doesn't propagate to child/async threads automatically (`InheritableThreadLocal` or `TaskDecorator` needed).
- Virtual threads make heavy ThreadLocal use costly; Java's **ScopedValue** is the modern alternative.

qa.q: How do you create a thread-safe Singleton?
Explain JVM memory areas. Where are objects, local variables and static variables stored?
qa.a:
- **Heap** (shared): all objects and arrays, the String pool; split into Young (Eden, S0, S1) and Old generations. GC operates here.
- **Metaspace** (native memory, Java 8+): class metadata, method bytecode, constant pool. Replaced PermGen, grows dynamically (cap with `-XX:MaxMetaspaceSize`).
- **Stack** (per thread): one frame per method call holding local primitives, object references, partial results. `StackOverflowError` on deep recursion.
- **PC register** and **native method stack** (per thread).

Where things live: objects -> heap; local primitives and references -> stack; static variables -> with the `Class` object on the heap (since Java 8; metadata in Metaspace). Instance fields -> inside the object on the heap.

qa.q: How does garbage collection work? Explain young and old generations.
qa.a:
GC frees memory of objects **unreachable from GC roots** (thread stacks' locals, static fields, JNI refs, active threads). It uses tracing, not reference counting, so cycles are collected.

Generational heap (most objects die young):
1. New objects are allocated in **Eden**.
2. When Eden fills, a **Minor GC** marks live objects and copies them to a Survivor space (S0/S1), incrementing their age. Eden is then wiped — cheap because most objects are dead.
3. Objects surviving enough cycles (tenuring threshold) are **promoted** to the **Old generation**.
4. When old gen fills, a **Major/Full GC** runs mark-sweep-compact — slower with longer stop-the-world pauses.

You can't force GC; `System.gc()` is just a hint. Tune with `-Xms/-Xmx`, choose collectors (`-XX:+UseG1GC`, `-XX:+UseZGC`), and analyse with GC logs (`-Xlog:gc*`).

qa.q: Compare G1 GC and ZGC. Which is the default?
qa.a:
**G1 (Garbage First)** — default since Java 9.
- Heap split into equal regions (1-32 MB) that can be Eden, Survivor, Old or Humongous.
- Concurrent marking; then evacuates regions with the most garbage first.
- Pause-time goal (`-XX:MaxGCPauseMillis`, default 200ms); typical pauses tens of ms.
- Good general-purpose choice for heaps from a few GB.

**ZGC** — production since Java 15, generational in Java 21 (default mode from 23).
- Almost everything (marking, relocation/compaction) is concurrent using coloured pointers and load barriers.
- Sub-millisecond pauses independent of heap size (up to 16 TB).
- Slightly lower throughput / higher CPU and memory overhead.
- Use for latency-sensitive services (trading, real-time APIs) and huge heaps.

Others: Parallel GC (max throughput, batch jobs), Serial (tiny heaps), Shenandoah (low-pause alternative).

qa.q: Explain class loading and the parent delegation model.
qa.a:
Class loading happens lazily, on first active use:
1. **Loading** — find the `.class` bytes and create a `Class` object.
2. **Linking** — *verify* bytecode, *prepare* static fields with defaults, *resolve* symbolic references.
3. **Initialization** — run static initialisers and static blocks.

Loaders: **Bootstrap** (core JDK, native), **Platform** (Java 9+, formerly Extension), **Application/System** (your classpath), plus custom ones (Tomcat, Spring Boot's `LaunchedURLClassLoader`).

**Parent delegation**: a loader delegates to its parent first and only loads itself if the parent fails. This guarantees core classes like `java.lang.String` always come from Bootstrap (security) and avoids loading duplicates. A class's identity is its name + its loader, so the same class loaded by two loaders gives `ClassCastException` between them.

qa.q: What causes OutOfMemoryError and how would you debug a memory leak in production?
qa.a:
Types: `Java heap space`, `GC overhead limit exceeded`, `Metaspace` (too many classes / classloader leaks), `unable to create native thread`, `Direct buffer memory`.

Common leak causes: unbounded static maps/caches, `ThreadLocal`s not removed in pools, listeners never deregistered, unbounded executor queues, holding large result sets (loading a whole table), unclosed resources.

Debug steps:
1. Enable `-XX:+HeapDumpOnOutOfMemoryError -XX:HeapDumpPath=/dumps`.
2. Watch heap/GC metrics (Actuator + Prometheus/Grafana, `jstat -gcutil`). A rising "floor" after each full GC indicates a leak.
3. Take a heap dump (`jcmd <pid> GC.heap_dump file.hprof`).
4. Analyse in Eclipse MAT/VisualVM: Leak Suspects report, dominator tree, path to GC roots.
5. Fix the code (bound caches with Caffeine, paginate queries), and add tests/alerts.

qa.q: StackOverflowError vs OutOfMemoryError?
qa.a:
- **StackOverflowError**: a thread's stack is exhausted, usually by infinite or very deep recursion (also cyclic `toString`/`hashCode` in bidirectional JPA entities or Jackson serialization loops). Fix the recursion or increase `-Xss`.
- **OutOfMemoryError**: the heap (or metaspace, native memory) can't satisfy an allocation even after GC. Caused by leaks or genuinely too much data. Fix by finding the leak, paginating/streaming data, or increasing `-Xmx`.

Both are `Error`s — don't catch them as normal flow.

qa.q: What is the JIT compiler?
qa.a:
The JVM starts by **interpreting** bytecode. The Just-In-Time compiler profiles execution and compiles **hot** methods (called frequently or with hot loops) into optimised native machine code stored in the code cache.

HotSpot uses **tiered compilation**: C1 (client compiler) compiles quickly with light optimisation; C2 (server compiler) later recompiles the hottest code with aggressive optimisations like inlining, escape analysis (allocating objects on the stack or eliminating them), loop unrolling, dead-code elimination, and lock elision. If assumptions break, code is deoptimised.

This is why Java apps "warm up" — early requests are slower. GraalVM native image (AOT) and CDS/CRaC are used to reduce startup time.

qa.q: What is serialization? What is serialVersionUID and transient?
qa.a:
Serialization converts an object graph into a byte stream (`ObjectOutputStream.writeObject`), and deserialization rebuilds it. Classes must implement the marker interface `Serializable`.
- **serialVersionUID**: a version number checked during deserialization. If the sender's and receiver's IDs differ, `InvalidClassException` is thrown. If you don't declare it, it's computed from the class structure, so any change breaks compatibility — always declare `private static final long serialVersionUID = 1L;`.
- **transient**: field is skipped (e.g. passwords, caches); it gets its default value after deserialization. `static` fields are also not serialized.
- A non-serializable field type causes `NotSerializableException`.
- `Externalizable` gives full manual control.
Java native serialization is a security risk with untrusted data; real systems use JSON/Protobuf/Avro.

qa.q: Is Java pass-by-value or pass-by-reference?
qa.a:
Java is **always pass-by-value**. For primitives the value is copied. For objects, the **reference** (a pointer value) is copied — so the method can mutate the object the reference points to, but reassigning the parameter doesn't change the caller's variable.
```java
void modify(List<Integer> list) {
    list.add(1);                 // visible to caller
    list = new ArrayList<>();    // only local copy changes
    list.add(2);                 // not visible to caller
}
```
That's why a classic `swap(a, b)` of two objects can't work in Java.

qa.q: What is the Integer cache? Why does `Integer a = 128, b = 128; a == b` return false?
qa.a:
Autoboxing uses `Integer.valueOf(int)`, which returns cached instances for values from **-128 to 127** (upper bound configurable with `-XX:AutoBoxCacheMax`). So `Integer a = 127, b = 127; a == b` is `true` (same object), but for 128 two different objects are created and `==` compares references, giving `false`.

`Long`, `Short`, `Byte`, `Character` (0-127) have similar caches; `Double`/`Float` don't.

Lesson: always compare wrapper objects with `equals()` or unbox first. Also, unboxing `null` (e.g. `int x = map.get(key)` when absent) throws `NullPointerException`.

qa.q: final vs finally vs finalize?
qa.a:
- **final** (keyword): a final variable can be assigned once; a final method can't be overridden; a final class can't be extended (e.g. `String`). A final reference can still point to a mutable object.
- **finally** (block): executes after try/catch regardless of exceptions — used for cleanup (now mostly replaced by try-with-resources).
- **finalize()** (method in `Object`): was called by the GC before reclaiming an object. Unpredictable, slow, could resurrect objects; deprecated since Java 9 and marked for removal. Use `AutoCloseable` or `java.lang.ref.Cleaner` instead.

qa.q: What is the difference between shallow copy and deep copy? How does clone() work?
qa.a:
- **Shallow copy** copies the object's fields as-is; reference fields still point to the same nested objects, so changes to nested objects are shared.
- **Deep copy** recursively copies nested mutable objects so the copy is fully independent.

`Object.clone()` performs a shallow, field-by-field copy and requires the class to implement `Cloneable` (otherwise `CloneNotSupportedException`). To deep copy you override `clone()` and clone mutable fields manually.

`clone()` is widely considered broken-ish (no constructor call, checked exception, casts). Prefer copy constructors or static factories:
```java
public Order(Order o) { this.id = o.id; this.items = new ArrayList<>(o.items); }
```
Or serialize/deserialize (e.g. via Jackson) for complex graphs.

qa.q: What are the main SOLID principles? Give an example of the Open/Closed principle.
What design patterns have you used in Java/Spring applications?
qa.a:
Pick ones you can explain with a real example:
- **Singleton** — Spring beans by default.
- **Factory** — `BeanFactory`, or a `PaymentProcessorFactory` returning an implementation by type.
- **Builder** — Lombok `@Builder`, `ResponseEntity.ok().header(...).body(...)`, `WebClient.builder()`.
- **Strategy** — interchangeable algorithms behind an interface (discounts, notification channels).
- **Template Method** — `JdbcTemplate`, `RestTemplate`: fixed skeleton, you supply callbacks.
- **Proxy** — Spring AOP proxies for `@Transactional`, `@Cacheable`, Hibernate lazy-loading proxies.
- **Observer** — Spring `ApplicationEvent`/`@EventListener`, Kafka pub-sub.
- **Adapter** — wrapping a third-party SMS SDK behind your own interface.
- **Decorator** — `BufferedInputStream` wrapping `InputStream`.
- **Chain of Responsibility** — Servlet filters / Spring Security filter chain.
Explain the problem it solved, not just the name.

qa.q: What is the difference between `==` and `equals()`?
qa.a:
- `==` compares **primitive values** or, for objects, **references** (are both variables pointing to the same object in memory?).
- `equals()` compares **logical content**, as defined by the class. `Object.equals` defaults to `==`; `String`, `Integer`, collections, records override it.
```java
String a = new String("x"), b = new String("x");
a == b;        // false
a.equals(b);   // true
```
For enums, `==` is fine and null-safe (singletons). For null-safe comparisons use `Objects.equals(a, b)`.

qa.q: What's new with interfaces in Java 8 and 9 (default, static, private methods)?
qa.a:
- **Default methods (8)**: methods with a body that implementations inherit, allowing interfaces to evolve without breaking existing implementers (`Collection.stream()`, `Iterable.forEach`).
- **Static methods (8)**: utility methods on the interface itself, called as `Comparator.naturalOrder()`; not inherited by implementing classes.
- **Private methods (9)**: share code between default methods without exposing it.

Diamond rule: if a class inherits the same default method from two interfaces, it must override it and can call a specific one with `InterfaceA.super.method()`. A class's own (or superclass's) method always wins over interface defaults.
